plan.contextChunk: This figure shows the geometry of light refraction at a planar interface between two optical media, as described by Snell's law. A horizontal black line divides the scene into an upper region with refractive index n1 and a lower region with refractive index n2; a thick blue line traces the ray direction as it strikes the interface and continues into the second medium. A thin vertical line marks the surface normal at the point of incidence, with a small right-angle square confirming its perpendicularity to the interface; the angle theta_1 is measured between the incoming ray and the normal above the interface, and theta_2 is measured between the refracted ray and the normal below. The ray bends toward or away from the normal depending on the relative magnitudes of n1 and n2, embodying the relationship n1 sin theta_1 = n2 sin theta_2. This figure introduces refraction geometry as the physical basis for how lenses bend light and form images.

interactionPlan.concept: Snell's law n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ governs how a light ray bends at an interface — toward the normal when entering a denser medium, away from it when entering a rarer one, and into total internal reflection past the critical angle when n₁ > n₂.
elements: horizontal black interface line separating the two media
upper medium label n₁ (left of the normal, above the interface)
lower medium label n₂ (left of the normal, below the interface)
thin vertical surface normal line through the point of incidence, labeled 'surface normal'
small right-angle square marker between the normal and the interface
thick blue incident ray arriving from the upper left, labeled 'ray direction'
thick blue refracted ray continuing into the lower medium, bent relative to the incident direction
thick blue reflected ray (visible only during total internal reflection), symmetric to the incident ray about the normal in the upper medium
angle arc θ₁ between the incident ray and the normal, with italic label θ₁
angle arc θ₂ between the refracted ray and the normal, with italic label θ₂
live readout of θ₁ and θ₂ in degrees near the arcs
critical-angle indicator/readout shown when n₁ > n₂

interactions.teaches: Angles are measured from the surface normal, and θ₂ is not independent — as the incident ray rotates about the interface point, the refracted ray re-aims itself continuously so that n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ always holds

interactions.label: n₁ (incident medium)
interactions.teaches: Raising n₁ relative to n₂ makes the ray bend away from the normal and is the precondition for total internal reflection

interactions.label: n₂ (transmitting medium)
interactions.teaches: Raising n₂ relative to n₁ bends the refracted ray closer to the surface normal; lowering it does the opposite

demo_steps.title: Bending toward the normal
demo_steps.narration: With n₁ = 1.0 (air) and n₂ = 1.5 (glass), the ray enters a denser medium and bends toward the normal — θ₂ < θ₁. Drag the incident ray and watch θ₂ track θ₁ exactly as Snell's law demands.

demo_steps.title: Stronger contrast, stronger bend
demo_steps.narration: Increase n₂ toward 2.0: the refracted ray hugs the normal ever more closely for the same θ₁ — the amount of bending is set by the ratio of indices, not by either one alone.

demo_steps.title: Bending away from the normal
demo_steps.narration: Swap the contrast — n₁ = 1.8, n₂ = 1.0. Now light speeds up crossing the interface and the refracted ray bends away from the normal, so θ₂ > θ₁.

demo_steps.title: Total internal reflection
demo_steps.narration: With n₁ > n₂, drag θ₁ past the critical angle θc = arcsin(n₂/n₁): no real θ₂ can satisfy Snell's law, so the refracted ray vanishes and a reflected ray appears symmetrically in the upper medium — all the light stays inside.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: θ₂ is slaved to θ₁ by n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, so when n₁ > n₂ there is a maximum θ₁ — the critical angle — beyond which no refracted ray can exist and light reflects totally inside the denser medium.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Match the textbook layout: horizontal black interface centered vertically, thin vertical normal through the incidence point with a right-angle square in the upper-right quadrant, 'surface normal' label at the top of that line, n₁ and n₂ labels stacked on the left side, incident ray entering from the upper left with the rotated 'ray direction' label alongside it, refracted ray exiting lower right and bent toward the normal in the default state (n₁=1.0, n₂=1.5). Rays are thick blue; the normal is a thinner, lighter blue. θ₁ and θ₂ are arc markers with italic serif labels placed between ray and normal. Dragging rotates the incident ray about the fixed incidence point (clamp θ₁ to roughly 0–90°); θ₂, its arc, and the refracted ray update live from Snell's law. When n₁ > n₂, show a critical-angle readout and a faint dashed marker at θc; once θ₁ exceeds θc, fade out the refracted ray and θ₂ arc, and fade in a reflected ray mirrored across the normal, optionally labeled 'total internal reflection'. At θ₁ = 0 the ray passes straight through undeviated — a useful anchor state. Keep the two index sliders visibly paired with their n₁/n₂ labels in the scene.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Drag the incident ray to change θ₁ and watch θ₂ update in real time according to n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, with both angle arc labels refreshing as the ray rotates about the interface point
- Sliders for refractive indices n₁ and n₂: show how increasing n₂ relative to n₁ bends the refracted ray closer to the surface normal, and vice versa
- Increase n₁ above n₂ and drag θ₁ past the critical angle to trigger total internal reflection, showing the refracted ray disappear below the interface and a reflected ray appear symmetrically above it

discrepancies: Generated figure adds gray angle arcs at θ₁ and θ₂ plus numeric degree readouts ('θ₁ = 40.0°', 'θ₂ = 25.4°') that do not appear in the source, which shows only the plain θ₁/θ₂ symbols
θ₂ label sits to the right of the refracted ray in the generated figure, whereas the source places it to the left of the ray, next to the normal
The refracted ray in the source ends well short of the bottom edge of the normal line; in the generated figure both rays extend beyond the normal's endpoints, slightly altering the composition
evaluation.notes: A faithful and pedagogically excellent Snell's-law figure: interface, normal, right-angle marker, both rays, and all source labels are present and correctly placed, and the drag-the-ray interaction plus n₁/n₂ sliders and TIR demo steps correctly enforce n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂; only the unrequested arcs/numeric readouts and minor label-position shifts differ from the source.
action_items: Clean up the redundant chain of three successive rdLabel.transform() calls (the first two are dead code with nonsense rotation expressions); keep a single rotate((t1*180/π)−180) so the 'ray direction' label reliably tracks the ray when dragged.
Consider dropping the numeric degree values from the default θ₁/θ₂ labels (or showing them only on hover/drag) so the default state reads as a closer drop-in for the static source.
Shorten the ray length so the rays terminate within the vertical extent of the normal line, matching the source composition.
